newsitem.title: UK: Britain to review law after Fred West film plan.
newsitem.headline: Britain to review law after Fred West film plan.

text.p: The British government said it would review the law after a row over plans for a movie about Fred and Rosemary West, the British couple who killed a series of women and girls to satisfy perverted sexual cravings.

The country's top judge said in a statement, made unexpectedly on the New Year public holiday, that the government would review the law governing the duties of the Official Solicitor, the legal official in charge of the West estate.
One newspaper said the company at the heart of the storm had now dropped plans for a film, a decision which it said would further embarrass the Official Solicitor, Peter Harris.
The Express quoted John Banks, a director of the London-based Portman Entertainment Group, as saying: "We will not be making the film." No one at Portman could be contacted for comment.

The Express said Banks explained that the film had been a pet project of a director who had now left the company. "Now he has gone, no one else in the company wants to make it. This decision was taken before the publicity," he said.

The announcement of the review by the Lord Chancellor, Lord Mackay, followed an outcry after the Official Solicitor decided to sell the rights to West's memoirs. Churchmen and members of parliament put pressure on the government to stop the sale.
But Harris said in a statement on Tuesday that it was the Official Solictitor's duty to "maximise the financial return to the estate" on behalf of West's five surviving children.
The Official Solicitor's duties include looking after the interests of children, the mentally ill and others who are unable to represent themselves in court proceedings.
Fred West was found hanged two years ago in a prison cell where he was awaiting multiple charges of murder and Rosemary West is serving 10 life jail sentences for murdering girls and young women.

Many of their victims were found buried in the garden and cellar of their house at 25 Cromwell Street in Gloucester, western England -- a building so notorious that officials not only knocked it down but ground its bricks into dust.
The local member of parliament, Douglas French, bitterly criticised the sale of the West memoirs, saying "common human decency" should be put before "commercial exploitation" of the case.

Harris confirmed on Tuesday that the Portman group had acquired an option to make the film. The option included access to tape recordings of police interviews with West, tapes of his favourite blue movies and pages of his memoirs written when awaiting trial.
